sections.h2: What makes selling a house in Olathe, KS different from the rest of Johnson County?
sections.html:
Olathe is the Johnson County seat, which means the county offices that record your deed and bill your taxes are inside the city. The 2020 census counted 141,290 residents, making Olathe the fourth most populous city in Kansas.

Most sellers here choose between a traditional listing, a sale without an agent, or a cash offer. The right route depends on the condition of the house and how soon you need to close. This guide covers the local facts that affect that choice.

sections.h2: How did Olathe grow from a trail stop to a city of 140,000?
sections.html:
John T. Barton founded Olathe in the spring of 1857, and the town was named the Johnson County seat in October 1859. Local lore says the name came from a Shawnee word for beautiful.

The early town lived off travelers on the Santa Fe, Oregon and California trails. The Mahaffie House, a wagon resupply point, is now a historic site run by the city. On September 6, 1862, William Quantrill's guerrillas raided Olathe and destroyed most of the town. The town then stayed small for decades.

Interstate 35 changed that in the 1950s by linking Olathe to Kansas City, Missouri. The census counts show the result: 10,987 people in 1960, 37,258 in 1980, 92,962 in 2000 and 141,290 in 2020. That is about 130,000 added residents in 60 years.

sections.h2: Where is Olathe and how do you get around it?
sections.html:
Olathe covers 60.42 square miles and borders Lenexa to the north, Overland Park to the east, De Soto to the northwest and Gardner to the southwest. Two public lakes sit inside the city: Lake Olathe at 172 acres of water and Cedar Lake at 45 acres.

Johnson County Transit runs a bus system through the county, including Olathe. A BNSF main line passes through the city. Johnson County Executive Airport, on about 500 acres with a 4,100-foot runway, is the second busiest airport in the state, and the closest airport with airline service is Kansas City International. The Federal Aviation Administration also operates the Kansas City air route traffic control center in Olathe.

Garmin, Olathe Public Schools, Olathe Health System, Johnson County Government and Farmers Insurance head the list in the city's 2022 financial report as summarized on Wikipedia. Honeywell, TransAm Trucking and the FAA also appear.

Farmers Insurance is based in Los Angeles, but Olathe has more of its employees than any other city in the United States. Olathe Public Schools says on its own site that it is a Forbes-recognized top employer.

  • Garmin International: the largest private employer in the city report.
  • Olathe Public Schools: the school district and one of the largest local payrolls.
  • Johnson County Government: courthouse, appraiser, treasurer and register of deeds.
  • FAA air route traffic control: a federal facility inside city limits.

sections.h2: Which school districts serve Olathe houses?
sections.html:
Five public districts reach into Olathe: Olathe USD 233, De Soto USD 232, Spring Hill USD 230, Blue Valley USD 229 and Gardner-Edgerton USD 231. Olathe USD 233 operates five high schools: Olathe North, South, East, Northwest and West.

If you live near a district line, the district named on your address matters to a buyer who is comparing homes. Check the district for your parcel before you describe it to anyone. MidAmerica Nazarene University and the Kansas School for the Deaf, founded in 1861, are also in Olathe.

sections.h2: What does Olathe's weather do to a house?
sections.html:
Olathe has a humid continental climate, with a January average high near 39 degrees and a July average high near 90. The temperature reaches 90 degrees about 36 days a year and 100 degrees about three days, and it falls below freezing on about 102 days.

Precipitation averages about 40 inches a year, most of it in May and June, and snowfall averages about 19 inches. The city's exterior maintenance code lists roofs, exterior surfaces, gutters, doors and windows among the items that must be kept in good condition, so a roof that has aged badly is both a buyer concern and a code issue.

sections.h2: What do Olathe's code and permit rules mean for a seller?
sections.html:
Olathe's Community Enhancement Division inspects properties for exterior code violations, and the city lists specific limits owners should know before showing a house.

  • Grass and weeds may not exceed eight inches.
  • Dead or diseased trees must come down, and limbs must stay above 13.5 feet over a street and 10 feet over a sidewalk.
  • Inoperable vehicles may not be stored outside, and tarps may not cover a vehicle.
  • Trash carts go to the curb after 5 p.m. the day before pickup and come in before 5 p.m. the next day.

After a complaint, an officer inspects, notifies the owner and sets a compliance time frame, which can be extended on request. If the owner does not comply, the city can abate the problem or send a notice to appear in Municipal Court. A seller with an open violation should clear it before closing so it does not pass to the buyer.

The residential permit page also says permits are not required for reroofing or for repairs down to the roof deck on one-family and two-family dwellings and townhomes, although the work must meet the current International Residential Code and the Olathe code. That helps an owner who wants to replace a roof before listing.

sections.h2: What should an Olathe landlord handle before selling?
sections.html:
Landlords selling in Olathe have a utility step to handle. The city says landlords on the automatic utility transfer program must call 913-971-9311 to cancel it if the property is sold, so the account does not keep reverting to the former owner.

Short-term rental hosts are asked to be considerate of neighbors, check any homeowners' association rules and follow city noise, trash and property maintenance codes. If the house is in an HOA, confirm those rules before you promise a buyer that a rental plan is allowed.

sections.h2: How do Johnson County property taxes and appeals work for an Olathe seller?
sections.html:
Johnson County lets owners pay in full by December 20 or in two installments, with the second half due May 10. The appraiser's office mails notices of appraised value on or before March 1, and the first chance to challenge a value is an informal appeal. The county's deadline table puts the filing date on or before March 31, which is 30 days after mailing under K.S.A. 79-1448.

Payment under protest has its own dates: December 20 if you pay the taxes yourself, January 31 if a mortgage company pays them, or May 10 for second-half or late full payments. If you are selling while an appeal is open, tell your closing agent so the protest paperwork stays with the right party.

sections.h2: What happens at the Johnson County Register of Deeds?
sections.html:
Deeds are recorded at the Register of Deeds in Olathe, at 111 S. Cherry St., Suite 1200. The office cannot accept documents by email or fax. Mail requires the original with payment and a stamped return envelope, and electronic recording is for title companies and law offices that have set up with the county.

Each deed needs a completed Kansas real estate sales validation questionnaire, and the questionnaire must follow the deed in the stack or processing is delayed. If the transfer is exempt, the exemption number must be on the deed.

sections.h2: When does a cash sale make sense in Olathe?
sections.html: A cash sale can make sense when the house has roof damage, a code notice, tenants or an estate attached to it, or when you need to close on a date a mortgage buyer could not meet. If the house is in good shape and you have time, a listing may reach more buyers. Contact us and we will tell you plainly where your house falls.

faqs.a: Olathe is in Johnson County, Kansas, and it is the county seat. The appraiser, treasurer and register of deeds serve Olathe from county offices in the city.

faqs.q: When are Johnson County property taxes due?
faqs.a: Taxes can be paid in full on or before December 20, or in two installments with the second half due May 10 of the following year, according to the Johnson County Treasury.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to replace a roof in Olathe?
faqs.a: Olathe's residential permit page says permits are not required for reroofing or repairs down to the roof deck on one-family and two-family dwellings and townhomes. The work still has to follow the adopted residential code and city code.

faqs.q: What is the Olathe weed height limit?
faqs.a: Grass and weeds may not exceed eight inches in height under the city's lawn maintenance code, and owners must also maintain adjacent right-of-way and easement areas within their property lines.

faqs.q: Where do I record a deed in Olathe?
faqs.a: At the Johnson County Register of Deeds, 111 S. Cherry St., Suite 1200. The office does not accept recordings by email or fax, and the deed must be accompanied by a sales validation questionnaire unless an exemption applies.

faqs.q: Can I sell my Olathe house with code violations?
faqs.a: Yes. An as-is sale is possible, but an open city violation affects the buyer, so clear it first or tell us about it upfront so it can be reflected in the number.
